claims.value: three cone types with different photopsins: S (420 nm), M (530 nm) and L (560 nm) cones
claims.quote: Some cones are maximally responsive to short light waves of 420 nm, so they are called S cones (“S” for “short”); others respond maximally to waves of 530 nm (M cones, for “medium”); a third group responds maximally to light of longer wavelengths, at 560 nm (L, or “long” cones).

source.citation: Clark MA, Douglas M, Choi J (2018). Biology 2e. OpenStax.

claims.quote: Opsin pigments are actually transmembrane proteins that contain a cofactor known as retinal. Retinal is a hydrocarbon molecule related to vitamin A.

claims.value: The cell splits its work in two: the inner segment holds the nucleus and everyday organelles, while the outer segment is specialized to capture light.
claims.quote: The inner segment contains the nucleus and other common organelles of a cell, whereas the outer segment is a specialized region in which photoreception takes place.

source.citation: Betts JG, Young KA, Wise JA, Johnson E, Poe B, Kruse DH, Korol O, Johnson JE, Womble M, DeSaix P (2022). Anatomy and Physiology 2e. OpenStax.

claims.value: Each of the three cone types carries an opsin tuned to different wavelengths, and the brain compares their activity to work out color.
claims.quote: The three types of cone opsins, being sensitive to different wavelengths of light, provide us with color vision. By comparing the activity of the three different cones, the brain can extract color information from visual stimuli.

source.citation: Betts JG, Young KA, Wise JA, Johnson E, Poe B, Kruse DH, Korol O, Johnson JE, Womble M, DeSaix P (2022). Anatomy and Physiology 2e. OpenStax.

claims.value: Cone opsins absorb light far less sensitively than rod rhodopsin, so cones serve vision in bright conditions while rods handle low light.
claims.quote: The absorbance of rhodopsin in the rods is much more sensitive than in the cone opsins; specifically, rods are sensitive to vision in low light conditions, and cones are sensitive to brighter conditions.

source.citation: Betts JG, Young KA, Wise JA, Johnson E, Poe B, Kruse DH, Korol O, Johnson JE, Womble M, DeSaix P (2022). Anatomy and Physiology 2e. OpenStax.

claims.value: Cones are only weakly light-sensitive and sit near the center of the retina; they respond to bright light and mainly serve daytime color vision.
claims.quote: Cones are weakly photosensitive and are located near the center of the retina. They respond to bright light, and their primary role is in daytime, color vision.

source.citation: Clark MA, Douglas M, Choi J (2018). Biology 2e. OpenStax.

claims.value: Cones are packed densely into the fovea, the central spot of the retina responsible for acute vision.
claims.quote: The fovea is the region in the center back of the eye that is responsible for acute vision. The fovea has a high density of cones.

source.citation: Clark MA, Douglas M, Choi J (2018). Biology 2e. OpenStax.

claims.value: Although less light-sensitive than rods, cones give vision finer spatial and temporal detail, and combining signals from cones with different pigments gives color vision.
claims.quote: Cones are less sensitive to light than rods, but they provide vision with higher spatial and temporal acuity, and the combination of signals from cones with different pigments allows color vision.

claims.value: Light-activated opsin switches on a G protein that shifts the cell's membrane potential, so the cell releases less neurotransmitter into the outer synaptic layer.
claims.quote: Activation of retinal and the opsin proteins result in activation of a G protein. The G protein changes the membrane potential of the photoreceptor cell, which then releases less neurotransmitter into the outer synaptic layer of the retina.

source.citation: Betts JG, Young KA, Wise JA, Johnson E, Poe B, Kruse DH, Korol O, Johnson JE, Womble M, DeSaix P (2022). Anatomy and Physiology 2e. OpenStax.

claims.value: In light the cone hyperpolarizes, which lifts its inhibition of bipolar cells.
claims.quote: Exposure of the retina to light hyperpolarizes the rods and cones and removes their inhibition of bipolar cells.

source.citation: Clark MA, Douglas M, Choi J (2018). Biology 2e. OpenStax.

tier1.text: Cone cells detect bright light and give us color vision during the day. Cones sit near the center of the retina, the light-sensing layer at the back of the eye. There are three kinds of cones, and each kind holds its own pigment, a molecule that absorbs light. The brain compares how active the three kinds of cones are to work out color.

tier2.text: Cone cells detect bright light and are used for color vision during the day. They sit near the center of the retina, the layer of light-sensing and supporting cells that lines the back of the eye. The fovea, the spot at the center of the retina that is responsible for sharp vision, has a high density of cones. Cones and rods, named for how they look, are the retina's two types of photoreceptor, receptor cells specialized to respond to light. Cones are less sensitive to light than rods, but cones give sharper vision in both space and time. A cone's outer segment, the part where light is detected, is cone-shaped and holds light-sensitive pigments in inward folds of the cell membrane. There are three cone pigments, called opsins, each sensitive to a particular wavelength of light, and they are specialized to perceive red, green and blue. The brain compares the activity of the three kinds of cones to work out color. Light alters the pigment molecule, and this changes the cone's membrane potential, the voltage difference between the inside and outside of the cell. A cone passes its signals to bipolar cells, which relay them to ganglion cells, and the ganglion cells carry the signal to the brain.
